result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.strongly_connected_components()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Get all strongly connected components as sets of node IDs. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L26311-L26388){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.strongly_connected_components() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Strongly connected components](/assets/graphs/strongly-connected-components.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A directed graph: a cycle A to B to C to A, a one-way edge C to D, a two-way pair D and E, and a separate one-way edge F to G. Following arrows, only the cycle and the two-way pair are mutually reachable, so there are four strong components, A, B, C in the accent color, D, E in teal, and the singletons F in violet and G in gold, listed on the card in the same colors." width="100%"} For directed graphs, a strongly connected component (SCC) is a maximal set of nodes where every node is reachable from every other node following directed edges. Uses Kosaraju's algorithm for efficient computation. For undirected graphs, returns the same result as `weakly_connected_components()` since strong connectivity equals regular connectivity when edges are bidirectional. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[set[int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of sets, where each set contains the node IDs in a strongly connected component. Components are returned in no particular order. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Kosaraju's algorithm (1978) computes SCCs in $O(V + E)$ time with three passes: first a DFS on the original graph produces a finish-time ordering, then the edge set is reversed, and a second DFS on the reversed graph in reverse-finish order carves out one SCC per tree it produces. The correctness argument is elegant: a node's SCC is exactly the set of vertices reachable from it in both $G$ and its transpose $G^ op$. Tarjan's algorithm delivers the same guarantee in a single DFS pass with an explicit stack; both are common choices, and any downstream code should treat the returned component list as unordered. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Nodes `A`, `B`, and `C` form a cycle, so each can reach the others and they collapse into one strongly connected component; `D` is reachable from the cycle but has no way back, so it forms its own component: ::: {#b0c2e432 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_node(label="A") .add_node(label="B") .add_node(label="C") .add_node(label="D") .add_edge("A", "B") .add_edge("B", "C") .add_edge("C", "A") # Creates a cycle -> SCC {A, B, C} .add_edge("C", "D") # D is reachable but can't reach back ) sccs = graph.strongly_connected_components() # Returns 2: {A, B, C} and {D} len(sccs) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: In a web graph, SCCs represent "communities" of mutually linked pages; finding the largest one highlights the biggest tightly-linked cluster: ::: {#d04ed4bc .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_node(label="A").add_node(label="B") .add_node(label="C").add_node(label="D") .add_edge("A", "B").add_edge("B", "C").add_edge("C", "A") # SCC of 3 .add_edge("C", "D") # D is a separate SCC ) sccs = graph.strongly_connected_components() largest_scc = max(sccs, key=len) # Returns 3 (A, B, C form the largest cluster) len(largest_scc) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 3 ``` ::: :::
